Les EMMIS – les brigades civiles sont-el: The EMMIS – Are Civilian Brigades the Solution to Social Tensions in Montréal?
La Ville vient d’annoncer le déploiement: The City has just announced that mobile social mediation and intervention teams will be deployed across the entire territory in early 2025.
Deux agents ÉMMIS en patrouille dans une: Two EMMIS agents on patrol on a Montréal street. Photo: Mathieu Sparks, Ville de Montréal
Il y a quelques semaines, un organisme c: A few weeks ago, a community organization confided in La Converse about its concerns following the announcement that civilian brigades would be deployed in every Montréal borough starting in 2025. According to this organization, the initiative caught community stakeholders by surprise and has raised worries within the community sector.
J’ai donc décidé de me pencher sur ces b: So I decided to look into these EMMIS brigades – the acronym stands for mobile social mediation and intervention teams (équipes mobiles de médiation et d’intervention sociale) – which are little known to the general public, even though they are aimed directly at the population. Who makes up these teams? What are their role and their powers? How are they managed? What indicators can be used to determine how effective they are? Is the community sector really opposed to this solution? For what reasons? These are the questions I set out to answer.
Pour cela j’ai rencontré les représentan: To do so, I met with representatives of several community organizations that work on social cohabitation issues, as well as a university professor who published a report on joint brigades and the EMMIS. I also asked the City to let me accompany a brigade in the field and to meet the three organizations that will be managing them. Unfortunately, after initially agreeing, the City postponed both meetings until early 2025.
<strong>Pour faire face à des enjeux soc: To address the social issues caused by homelessness and youth violence in Montréal, the City has just announced that mobile social mediation and intervention teams (EMMIS) will be deployed across the entire territory in early 2025. The decision has been criticized by some community organizations. La Converse breaks down this pilot project – and its limits.
À l’heure du dîner, vendredi dernier, al: At lunchtime last Friday, as the last dead leaves fall on the asphalt of Maisonneuve Boulevard in the Village, one man draws attention. Dressed in worn clothes, his face irritated by the cold of early winter, he shouts incomprehensible words, walks into the middle of traffic and opens his pants to urinate in full view of everyone. A few metres away, two police officers barely turn toward this man, who is visibly experiencing homelessness and mental distress, while passersby look away and quicken their pace. A few hours later in Saint-Michel, two groups of youths under 16 hurl insults at each other in an alley. It is hard to tell what the altercation is about. As tension rises and curses fly, a father walking by with his daughter slows down, then crosses to the other side of the street.
Ce genre de scènes ne survient pratiquem: Scenes like these almost never happen in much of Montréal, but they are occurring more and more often in certain hot spots. By announcing that mobile social mediation and intervention teams (EMMIS) will be implemented in all 19 of the city’s boroughs next year, the municipal administration has decided to tackle social cohabitation issues.
« Nous sommes tous témoins de situations: “We are all witnessing difficult situations in public space. We see more homelessness, more mental health crises, more marginalized groups and more poverty,” Montréal Mayor Valérie Plante said at a press conference on August 13, 2023. “Businesses have shared their concerns and feel helpless when faced with delicate situations. There are also worried citizens, and we have to listen to them; but we also have to find solutions that are both pragmatic and caring.”
Certains citoyens et commerçants se plai: Some residents and merchants complain of noise, gatherings, human waste, or people under the influence of alcohol or drugs… It was in response to the fed-up feelings of some Montrealers that the City launched the EMMIS in 2021 as a pilot project in the boroughs of Ville-Marie and Sud-Ouest. Last year, the teams’ services were then extended to the métro and to a few boroughs particularly affected by homelessness, such as Plateau-Mont-Royal and Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, where a total of 52 workers were deployed.
Quand on songe à l’itinérance, l’image d: When we think of homelessness, the image of a person living on the street or in a shelter immediately comes to mind. Yet, far from this cliché, homelessness is diverse, as are the factors that lead to it. Financial hardship, violence, health problems, eviction, substance use, job loss and family breakdown are just some of the causes that can derail a life path. This social tragedy is affecting older and older people, and among those experiencing homelessness, Indigenous people, men, LGBTQ+ youth, immigrants and asylum seekers are overrepresented. The proportion of women has also risen in recent years, reaching 29% in 2022, according to Statistics Canada.
En 2021, plus d’un Canadien sur 10 (11,2: In 2021, more than one in 10 Canadians (11.2%), or 1,690,000 people, reported having experienced homelessness at some point in their lives, again according to Statistics Canada. Montréal is no exception. The metropolis accounts for 47% of the people experiencing homelessness counted in 2022, which represented 4,690 people at the time. That figure is widely underestimated, according to several community organizations, and does not account for hidden homelessness – which refers to people who are staying with friends or sleeping in their cars.
La Ville assure que les escouades civile: The City insists that the civilian squads to be deployed across the island will not be limited to the issue of homelessness. “The mandate of the EMMIS is to provide a social response to social cohabitation issues related to the sharing of space. It is therefore not limited to issues related to homelessness. In this context, the social cohabitation in question refers to living together between people or groups who do not share the same characteristics, needs or perspectives, provided that these differences (or disputes) stem either from social vulnerabilities – homelessness, residential instability, mental health, addictions – or from the marginalization of certain groups of individuals because of their age or their socio-economic or immigration status,” the City says.
Les phénomènes de délinquance et de viol: Delinquency and gun violence have indeed increased among young Montrealers. They are also the primary victims, with <l1>dozens of deaths</l1> of people under 17 to mourn in recent years. This causes worry among parents, and irritation among some residents and business owners, particularly near places where young people tend to gather.
Du côté des organismes, la perplexité es: Among community organizations, bewilderment has been evident since the presentation of the EMMIS’ broader target audience. “Honestly, I didn’t even know they wanted to tackle youth-related issues. I have some doubts about the relevance of this project, and it’s all very vague for us. The Coalition Pozé [an organization involved in the upcoming deployment of the EMMIS squads, Editor’s note] plans to come and give a presentation at our next meeting, so we hope to get answers then,” confides Sabrina Fauteux, executive director of Concertation Saint-Léonard.
Ce qui devait être une bonne nouvelle pr: What was supposed to be good news is, in fact, causing some grumbling. “The idea of having people who don’t carry weapons intervene with populations in precarious situations is interesting in itself, because today it’s police officers who intervene, even though they are a historic symbol of violence for these communities and their actions are necessarily repressive,” says Jeremy Lamarche, representative of the Réseau d’aide aux personnes seules et itinérantes de Montréal (RAPSIM).
Il montre notamment du doigt le fonction: In particular, he points to how these brigades operate and the fact that they fall under the institutional authority of the City, which could, in effect, have “a bias,” he says. “The EMMIS respond to complaints from residents and merchants, which still puts them in a repressive position. The needs of these people aren’t being taken into account; the problem is just being moved somewhere else,” he laments.
De son côté, la municipalité avance des: For its part, the municipality points to evidence that this approach works.
La Ville et le ministère de la Sécurité: The City and Quebec’s Ministry of Public Security are investing $50 million over five years to deploy 90 EMMIS agents in Montréal’s 19 boroughs. A 211 telephone assistance line will be set up starting in January to dispatch the EMMIS, and deployment in the new boroughs will be gradual.
La Ville va collaborer avec des organism: The City will work with organizations “already well established in their communities” to develop its EMMIS program. It says the Coalition Pozé, which is already active in the northeast of the metropolis, “will draw on its expertise in working with Montréal youth.” The Société de développement social, which works downtown, will also be involved, as will Équijustice, which already does social mediation.
Concrètement, ces brigades sont composée: In practice, these brigades are made up of two psychosocial workers who travel by car. Four conditions must be met for an intervention to begin: the situation is non-urgent, meaning it presents no immediate danger; it involves a social cohabitation issue (incivilities, use of public space, etc.); it involves “social vulnerabilities”: homelessness, addictions, mental health, marginalization based on age; and it takes place in Montréal’s public space.
Les EMMIS seront envoyées sur le terrain: The EMMIS will be sent into the field by dispatch operators who will answer calls to the 211 assistance line based on these criteria. The goal is to spare police from having to respond to non-priority situations. Once on site, the teams’ mission is to try to find a solution to the problem. It could be a person urinating in the street, a group of people being too noisy, an encampment, or someone using substances in public space.
Cependant, ces intervenants psychosociau: However, these psychosocial workers have no police powers. “In practical terms, the EMMIS carry out three types of intervention: social mediation, social intervention and prevention,” the City explains. “It is important to specify that EMMIS interventions are voluntary. If the person concerned does not agree to be helped, to change their behaviour, to leave the premises or to take part in a social mediation process, the team must end its intervention.”
Selon la Ville, le projet pilote aurait: According to the City, the pilot project has proven itself and produced conclusive results. Montréal says daily calls to the EMMIS teams doubled over the past year, with 15% of requests coming from residents and businesses. In 2023, more than 15,000 interventions were carried out in the four boroughs where EMMIS were present. Finally, from February to June, the EMMIS were called to intervene in the métro 1,075 times.
Des chiffres sur lesquels semble être fo: These figures appear to be the basis for Mayor Valérie Plante’s political decision to extend the model across all of Montréal. However, beyond the number of calls and interventions, no data has been released that would allow an assessment of the civilian brigades’ impact or of any decrease in social cohabitation problems.
L’année dernière, un rapport consacré au: Last year, a report on joint brigades and the EMMIS, on the other hand, pointed to certain limits of this initiative and raised several risks.
Ted Rutland revient sur le rapport qu'il: Ted Rutland discusses the report he led on joint and civilian brigades, including the EMMIS. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy, La Converse
<strong>« Une couche de plus pour la sur: “One more layer of surveillance for marginalized people in public space”
Ted Rutland, professeur agrégé du départ: Ted Rutland, associate professor in the Department of Geography, Planning and Environment at Concordia University, studied the EMMIS pilot project at the request of RAPSIM and published a report in September 2023. Titled Innovation ou extension de la répression ? Perspectives des intervenant-es sur les escouades mixtes à Montréal, it draws on interviews with 38 workers from several Montréal community organizations.
« L’objectif de ce rapport était d’étudi: “The aim of this report was to study the relevance of these squads. I led the research with two students, and RAPSIM helped me get access to workers for the interviews,” Ted Rutland explains. “I have no interest in criticizing an initiative that helps improve the situation even minimally, but these interviews brought to light several problems with the joint squads, made up of civilian workers and police officers, and with the EMMIS.”
La première limite soulevée par M. Rutla: The first limit raised by Rutland concerns the EMMIS interventions, which start from citizens’ complaints. “The joint squads remain rooted in a logic of repression that aims to satisfy the interests of certain residents and merchants who don’t want to see poverty, to the detriment of the needs of people experiencing homelessness,” the researcher explains.
Un constat partagé par Sabrina Fauteux,: Sabrina Fauteux, executive director of Concertation Saint-Léonard, a coalition that brings together several neighbourhood organizations, shares this view. “It’s really one more layer of surveillance for marginalized people in public space, with a strategy of moving people along to respond to complaints from housed citizens, who will feel like the City is taking concrete action. That’s politics, not mediation,” she says.
Selon le rapport, ce fonctionnement aura: According to the report, this way of operating has the effect of maintaining a one-way “repressive approach.” It also calls the aim of resolving social cohabitation problems through one-off interventions “utopian.” “These squads are supposed to deliver an immediate solution within a few hours at most. That is very different from the time scale of street outreach work, which is generally long-term because of the very nature of the work,” Rutland says. “The squads’ short-term orientation translates into indicators of success like the number of interventions or the number of people reached – figures that say nothing about the outcome of the intervention or the long-term effects of the work,” he adds. According to stakeholders in the field, time is a sine qua non for any intervention with people experiencing homelessness.
« On attend vraiment qu’on nous présente: “We’re really waiting for things to be presented to us clearly, because it’s still very vague. What power do they have during an intervention? Say two EMMIS agents go up to youths playing basketball because someone complained about the noise; they ask them to leave, and then what? They’ll go up to a person experiencing homelessness, ask them to leave, and then what? At best, they will have moved the problem to the next street over,” Sabrina Fauteux points out.
<strong>« On a vu beaucoup de personnes: “We’ve seen a lot of people lose trust in us”
Autre point dénoncé par une partie du mi: Another point denounced by part of the community sector: the danger it poses to their work. By intervening on a one-off basis with the same populations without being easily identifiable, the EMMIS would be undermining the work of street outreach workers. “Even though this squad is made up entirely of civilians, several workers say the EMMIS also create a hostile environment for people experiencing homelessness,” Rutland points out. “These people are already in a situation of great vulnerability and they don’t necessarily understand who the EMMIS are. They think these teams are with the police or that they are street outreach workers.”
Un problème dont la mairie est conscient: City Hall is aware of the problem. “Over-intervention is a concern for the EMMIS, which is why we are making efforts to coordinate with field workers who assist people in vulnerable situations. This approach aims to make the service complementary to the ecosystem, whether by filling service gaps, reinforcing joint actions or relieving partners of certain interventions. All of this is done while respecting the mandates of each party,” the City says.
Mais, à Ville-Marie, où une EMMIS est pr: But in Ville-Marie, where an EMMIS team has been present since 2021 and where homelessness is a real issue, Alexandra Pontbriand, director of Spectre de rue, is already noting negative effects. “Since they started intervening, we’ve seen a lot of people lose trust in us, because the EMMIS present themselves as social workers, but they don’t do the same work at all. Besides, they aren’t bound by a strict code of confidentiality like street outreach workers are, who never reveal the content of their conversations with the people they serve… It also creates over-solicitation, when people experiencing homelessness are already approached a great deal in public space, and it can take us days to find them again, because an EMMIS team made them leave. We don’t know where they’ve set up again and we can’t continue our follow-up,” says the woman, who speaks “on behalf of the Regroupement des organismes communautaires québécois pour le travail de rue (ROCQTR).”
Les organismes communautaires craignent: Community organizations fear their mission will be replaced by that of these squads, which take a completely different approach. “Workers raise this replacement mainly when it comes to funding, describing ‘unfair’ funding that would be taken from envelopes that should be going to them. Several workers cite projects that fell through because of a lack of funding and long-term stability,” Ted Rutland notes. “Some workers say they have lost partners, shares of funding and programs since these squads were put in place,” the researcher adds.
Interrogée sur ces craintes, la Ville s’: Asked about these fears, the City sought to reassure: “The City of Montréal recognizes and appreciates the essential work that community groups do. These organizations play a crucial role in supporting people in vulnerable situations and promoting social cohesion. The creation of the mobile social mediation and intervention team (EMMIS) is not intended to replace these efforts, but rather to complement them.”
La perte de financement des organismes e: The loss of funding for organizations and their growing difficulty in renewing their projects are concerns that come up every year. So the announcement of $50 million over five years for the EMMIS has gone over badly. “A colossal budget is being given to something that hasn’t proven itself, instead of putting these resources toward organizations already active in social cohabitation and homelessness, which have decades of experience in the field and of accountability reporting that prove their impact,” Sabrina Fauteux says.
Autrement dit, la Ville alloue des moyen: In other words, the City is allocating funds to brigades whose action is limited by their very nature, while the amounts devoted to projects that could resolve or ease the underlying problems behind social cohabitation issues are insufficient. These problems include the housing crisis, youth violence, mental and physical health disorders, the lack of space in shelters, and more. In 2024, the City spent $6.5 million on homelessness, compared with $10 million for the EMMIS brigades, which it presents as “one solution among many.”
